list.listitem: For evaluation of suspected osteoarthritis (OA), order weight-bearing anterior views. C
Acetaminophen and NSAIDS should be the first-line drug treatment for OA; opiates should be avoided.A.

The 2020 ACR guidelines made strong recommendations for a comprehensive approach to hip or knee OA that includes exercise, self-efficacy programs, weight loss, tai chi, and assistive devices (eg, canes, tibiofemoral knee braces, and thumb splints). The panel made conditional recommendations in favor of education, cognitive behavioral therapy, and other forms of exercise. B

The 2020 American College of Radiology guidelines on knee and hip OA made strong recommendations against the use of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, platelet-rich plasma or stem cell injections, chondroitin (knee, hip), and intra-articular hyaluronic acid (hip). B
Arthroscopic debridement for treatment of OA and surgery for non-traumatic meniscal tears are not effective. Total knee arthroplasty is effective when indicated based on pain and function. A

background.definition: Osteoarthritis (OA), also known as degenerative joint disease (DJD), is articular soft tissue and cartilage deterioration associated with reactive bony changes. These degenerative changes can lead to pain, loss of joint motion, and subsequent disability. OA can affect one or many joints.

list.listitem: The prevalence of OA is 21.6% of the adult US population (46.4 million persons).
A systematic review of radiographic study of hip OA provided a range of estimates from 0.9% to 27% with a mean of 8%.
OA is the most common form of arthritis and has an estimated annual cost of $95 billion dollars.
Genetic predisposition. GDF5 rs143383 polymorphism is strongly associated with knee OA.
Older than 50 years; increases with aging.
Acute or recurrent trauma.
Excessive and prolonged physical stress to the joint.
Obesity can lead to OA in weight-bearing joints.
Knucklecracking does not cause osteoarthritis of the hand joints.

OA results when the rate of cartilage degeneration exceeds routine chondrocyte remodeling. An altered repair response results in osteophyte and subchondral cyst formation, which leads to further cartilage loss.
Joint pain results in decreased joint use and a further loss of physiologic stimulation of chondrocyte activity. This process further impairs joint tissue function.
Synovitis may be responsible for pain.
For the evaluation of knee OA, take a weight bearing anterior view to determine loss of joint space. C
A standing posteroanterior view radiograph with the knee flexed to 45° can show cartilage loss of the posterior aspect of the knee. C

Differential.Differential_Features: More swelling and erythema than in OA
Usually affects foot/ankle and can affect knees in later disease
Nonbirefringent crystals on microscopy, presentation can vary
May have elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated rheumatoid factor, periarticular erosions, affect proximal interphalangeal joints
Radiographic changes in cervical and lumbar spine
Skin changes and erosions on distal interphalangeal joints
Fever, inability to move joint secondary to patient guarding/pain
Tick bite history; rash; other systemic symptoms, such as adenopathy

list.listitem: Cartilage space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis may be present.
See .

Patients typically complain of pain or tenderness exacerbated by activity and relieved by rest. Morning stiffness usually lasts less than 30 minutes, but may recur during periods of inactivity. Symptoms may be affected by changes in weather. The onset of symptoms is usually not acute or severe. Involved joints are most commonly fingers, knees, hips, and spines.

On physical examination, patients often have joint swelling and crepitus may be present. In late stages, there is joint deformity. Usually there is no erythema or fever. Pain, joint swelling, stiffness, and functional limitation are common. Severe local inflammation, erythema, and progressive pain suggest other diagnoses.
Individual symptoms that best rule in OA are pain during flexion, functional limitation, and bony enlargement. Being younger than 50 years reduces the likelihood of OA.

A systematic review concluded that symptoms associated with hip OA include family history, pain climbing stairs or walking down slopes, and concomitant knee pain (all with LR+ near 2.0), and worst pain in the medial thigh (LR+ 7.8). Symptoms that reduce the likelihood of hip OA include younger age, less than 60 minutes of morning stiffness, no pain with walking, and pain not improved by sitting. Physical findings that increase the likelihood of hip OA include posterior hip pain with squatting (LR+ 6.1), groin pain on hip abduction or adduction (LR+ 5.7), abductor weakness (LR+ 4.4), decreased hip adduction (LR+ 4.2) and decreased internal rotation (LR+ 3.2). A limitation is that most of the studies used radiography as the reference standard, and other studies have shown that the correlation between radiographic findings of the hip and hip pain are inconsistent.

According to the European League for Rheumatism (EULAR), three symptoms (persistent knee pain, limited morning stiffness, and reduced function) and three signs (crepitus, restricted movement, and bony enlargement) are the most useful in the diagnosis of knee OA. EULAR guidelines recommend that typical symptoms in a patient with risk factors for OA should “overrule” a normal radiograph when making the diagnosis.
EULAR guidelines note that in patients with risk factors for OA an typical symptoms, imaging is not necessarily required. Effusions should be aspirated to rule out other causes for joint pain.

Cartilage space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis may be present on radiographs. Radiography is used to monitor disease progression, assess patients with symptoms lasting several weeks, or to rule out other disorders. The specific views to order for different joints are listed below.

It is important to remember that abnormalities are common on MRI studies of the knee, spine, and other joints, but these patients are often asymptomatic. In fact, one study of adults older than 50 years without clinically diagnosed osteoarthritis found that about 90% had knee damage on MRI.

A meta-analysis of studies of MRI in patients with hip and knee pain concluded that for the knee, synovitis, bone marrow edema-like lesions, and joint effusions seen on MRI were associated with symptoms. Meniscal tears were not informative and did not necessarily respond to surgery. MRI of the hip was useful to diagnose femoroacetabular impingment, labral tears, and chondral lesions that responded to surgery.

A study performed an MRI in 115 sedentary adults without knee pain or impaired function. Almost all knees had at least one structural abnormality, with meniscal tear (usually medial) seen in 30% and meniscal deterioration in another 18%. Moderate to severe cartilage abnormalities were seen in 41% of participants. About one third had a Baker's cyst, and 26% had prepatellar bursitis. Seeing these findings in symptomatic persons should therefore be interpreted with caution.

Also, the correlation between radiographic indicators of hip arthritis and hip pain is very low. Hip pain is not present in many hips with radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis, and many people with painful hips, including older patients with groin or anterior pain and/or painful internal rotation, will not have indicators on x-ray.
Spine: anteroposterior.
Hip: anteroposterior (weight-bearing).

Knee: Standard protocols include anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique views. For the evaluation of knee OA, a weight-bearing anteroposterior view should be taken to evaluate the loss of joint space. The lateral view is used to assess femoral condyles and patella. Standing posteroanterior view with the knee flexed to 45°, also known as tunnel view, is used to assess intra-articular loose bodies or chondral defects, and can assess cartilage loss of the posterior aspect of the knee. Merchant views are used to assess patellofemoral pathology.
Hand: anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique.
Ankle: mortise view, anteroposterior, and lateral.
Shoulder: anteroposterior, lateral, and scapular Y views.

OA is likely in older patients with insidious onset in commonly affected joints with joint pain, swelling, and morning stiffness. Swelling may be present on physical examination, along with tenderness and crepitus.
In the presence of acute pain accompanied by swelling, erythema, fever, or rash, consider septic arthritis, Lyme disease, or gout.
Consider radiologic studies after prolonged symptoms or if a fracture or a tumor is suspected.
Acetaminophen and NSAIDS should be the first-line treatment for OA, with a non-opioid strategy preferred over an opioid based strategy.A

Avoid NSAIDs in patients with prior gastrointestinal ulcers or bleeding, and in patients taking warfarin and/or corticosteroids. If NSAIDs produce gastrointestinal symptoms add a proton pump inhibitor.A
A steroid injection is an effective short-term treatment for knee and hip OA.B
The best designed studies conclude that arthroscopy and hyaluronic acid injections are unlikely to be effective. A

The 2020 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guidelines made strong recommendations for a comprehensive approach to hip or knee OA that includes exercise, self-efficacy programs, weight loss, tai chi, and assistive devices (eg, canes, tibiofemoral knee braces, and thumb splints). The panel made conditional recommendations in favor of education, cognitive behavioral therapy, and other forms of exercise. B

The 2020 ACR guidelines on knee and hip OA made strong recommendations against the use of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, bisphosphonates, glucosamine, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, biologicals, platelet-rich plasma or stem cell injections, chondroitin (knee, hip), and intra-articular hyaluronic acid (hip). B
Ice massage can improve range of motion and function in knee OA, as can low-intensity aerobic exercise. and Swedish massage.B

The 2019 American College of Rheumatology guidelines on hand, knee and hip OA made strong recommendations for topical NSAIDs for knee OA, oral NSAIDs. Conditional recommendations were made for acetaminophen, duloxetine, and tramadol. They made strong recommendations against the use of bisphosphonates, glucosamine, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and biologicals.
Acetaminophen is the first-line treatment in patienapts older than 65 years. Continuous doses of 4 g per day are often necessary to control symptoms.
NSAIDs are all equally effective for OA. Patients with Helicobacter pylori and/or a history of dyspepsia should be treated with a proton pump inhibitor while taking NSAIDs.

To reduce bleeding risk, avoid NSAID use in patients with prior gastrointestinal ulcers or bleeding and in patients taking warfarin and/or corticosteroids. The COX-2 inhibitor celecoxib has a similar risk of serious adverse gastrointestinal effects as other NSAIDs in long-term users. Gastrointestinal symptoms from NSAID use can be controlled with an antacid, H2 blocker, or preferably a proton pump inhibitor.
The chronic use of COX-2 inhibitors is associated with an increased cardiovascular risk.

Tramadol alone or in combination with acetaminophen has no important overall benefit on mean pain or function in people with osteoarthritis compared to placebo. Although slightly more people in the tramadol group report important improvements in pain or function, adverse events are higher with tramadol.
The use of non-tramadol opiates is not routinely recommended due to the increased risk for adverse events.

An RCT randomized 240 patients with chronic back, hip or knee osteoarthritis that was at least moderately severe to an opioid or non-opioid pain management strategy. The opioid group began with immediate releast oral opioids, then sustained release oral opioids, and finally transdermal fentanyl if needed. The non-opioids used a stepped approach that included acetaminophen and NSAIDs, amitriptylline or gabapentin, topical analgesics, and finally pregabalin, duloxetine, or tramadol. There was no difference between groups in pain related function, and pain intensity was significantly better in the non-opioid group. Dropouts due to adverse effects were more common in the opioid group.
A Cochrane review of opioids for chronic non-cancer pain concluded that while many patients discontinue opioids, a subset are able to continue using them long-term with good pain relief.

A randomized trial in 407 persons with moderate to severe OA found that once weekly semaglutide resulted in a change in the WOMAC pain score of 42 points compared with 27 points in the placebo group. This difference was both statistically and clinically significant. Weight loss was the likely mediator.

A 2025 randomized trial found that metformin (titrated to 2000 mg daily) significantly reduced knee pain compared to placebo in adults with overweight/obesity and knee osteoarthritis (but without diabetes) over 6 months. While statistically significant, the reduction in pain scores (-11.4 mm) did not meet the pre-specified threshold for clinical importance (15 mm). Notably, weight loss was similar between groups, suggesting a direct anti-inflammatory mechanism.
Capsaicin is effective for some patients when used chronically.
It should be noted in interpretation of clinical trials, that placebo is effective in reducing pain and stiffness and in improving self-reported function for patients with OA.

Vitamin D targeted to reach plasma levels greater than 36 ng/mL for 2 years had no effect on osteoarthritic knee pain or changes in MRI imaging for cartilage thickness or lesion size in the bone marrow among 146 participants with symptomatic osteoarthritis.
A systematic review of 33 trials with 5318 participants found no evidence that antidepressants reduce OA pain.

A study randomized 4113 patients to cefazolin + vancomycin or cefazolin + placebo following total knee or hip arthroplasty. For TKA rates of surgical site infection were 5.7% in the vancomycin group and 3.7% in the placebo group (RR 1.5, 95% CI 1.04-2.2). There was no difference for THA (3.0% for vancomycin vs 3.1%.

A trial randomized 207 participants with knee OA to oral methotrexate once weekly (escalating from 10 to 25 mg over 6 weeks) or placebo. After 6 months, reduction in pain from baseline was significantly higher in the methotrexate group (0.8 point greater reduction on a 10 point scale). However, this change is of marginal if any clinical significance.

The 2019 American College of Rheumatology guidelines on knee and hip OA made strong recommendations against the use of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, platelet-rich plasma or stem cell injections, chondroitin (knee, hip), and intra-articular hyaluronic acid (hip). They made a strong recommendation for intraarticular corticosteroid injections for knee OA. Conditional recommendations were made for radiofrequency ablation for knee OA, and for intraarticular steroid injections and chondroitin sulfate injections for hand OA,

Joint replacement is an important treatment option for patients with severe osteoarthritis. Obese patients (BMI >30) are not at as great a risk of hardware failure after total joint replacement as previously thought.
Most hip and knee replacements last up to 25 years.

A systematic review found no evidence that increased physical activity after knee replacement is associated with failure of the joint, although different activities (swimming and running and tennis) were lumped together as "high intensity".
Obese patients (BMI >30) are not at as great a risk of hardware failure after total joint replacement as previously thought.
High tibial osteotomy is effective for unicompartmental knee OA.
Resurfacing hip arthroplasty in three clinical trials had similar or better outcomes than total hip arthroplasty at short- to midterm follow-up.

Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) represents adverse morphology of the hip predisposing to premature joint degeneration. FAI occurs in about 20% of the general population, 25% of which will develop pain or osteoarthritis. 222 participants with symptomatic FAI were randomized to arthroscopic hip surgery or physical therapy and activity modification. Hip outcome scores of the daily living subscale were approximately 10 points higher with surgery compared to physical therapy.

A study randomized 4113 patients to cefazolin + vancomycin or cefazolin + placebo following total knee or hip arthroplasty. For TKA rates of surgical site infection were 5.7% in the vancomycin group and 3.7% in the placebo group (RR 1.5, 95% CI 1.04-2.2). There was no difference for THA (3.0% for vancomycin vs 3.1%.
A trial randomized 121 patients undergoing TKA to inlay, onlay round, or onlay oval patellar implant. THose in the onlay round group had better patient reported pain and function outcomes.

A series of 300 consecutive patients who underwent bilateral knee TKA found no difference in outcomes between joints with and without retention of the posterior cruciate ligament (94% survival in both groups at 19.5 years%).

In a study with some methodological issues, total hip replacement (THR) significantly improved hip function over exercise at 6 months (+15.9 vs. +4.5 Oxford Hip Score, P < .001), although 21% of the exercise group crossed over to THR.
Arthroscopy with arthroscopic debridement and lavage is not an effective treatment for OA of the knee.
In one RCT, arthroscopic surgery plus medical and physical therapy was no more effective than medical and physical therapy alone.

No significant difference was noted among 351 adult patients with a non-traumatic meninscal tear after 12 months who were treated with arthroscopic surgery plus physical therapy vs physical therapy alone. However, 30% of the patients initially assigned to PT ultimately had surgery within 6 months.
In another study of 146 patients with non-traumatic medical meniscus tears, no differences were noted in patients randomized to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy versus sham surgery after 12 months.

Autologous chondrocyte implantation for patients with a full thickness defect of the knee (ie, implanting their own cartilage) has only been studied in several small, poorly designed trial with mixed results.
One small RCT with with unbalanced randomization concluded that ACI was more effective than mosaicplasty for defects of knee articular cartilage.
Another with 80 patients found no difference between ACI and microfracture in patients with cartilage defect on the femoral condyle.
Corticosteroid injections are effective. A systematic review found duration of pain reduction was 2 to 4 weeks. The same joint should not be treated more than 4 times per year.

In a randomized clinical trial of 40 milligrams of triamcinolone injection (vs saline) every 3 month for two years, no differences in clinical outcomes were noted in those receiving triamcinolone, and triamcinolone injections were associated with great cartilage loss as assessed by MRI (0.21 mm v 0.10 mm). However, pain was measured 3 months after each injection, which is longer than the benefit is thought to last.

A trial randomized patients to IM or intraarticular corticosteroid injection using the same drug and dose (triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg). Intraarticular was slightly better at 1 month but IM was slightly better at 2 months. Overall differences were small and probably not clinically significant. Unfortunately there was no placebo injection.

A systematic review multiple corticosteroid injections with other injections. Combining all studies, they found a small to moderate improvement in pain with steroid injections (0.5 standardized mean differences) but also some harms including loss of joint space and an association with the need for joint replacement surgery. However, the latter could well be due to confounding by indication.

A network meta-analysis (16 studies, 1809 participants) of injections for hip osteoarthritis concluded that the only effective drug was corticosteroids for short term pain reduction, but not at 6 months or longer.
A cost-effectiveness analysis found that ultrasound guided corticosteroid injections for hip OSA were highly cost-effective with lower healthcare costs and higher QALYs than best usual care.
Stem cell injections

A systematic review identified 8 RCTs comparing mesenchymal stromal stem cell (MSC) injections with placebo and 5 RCTs comparing it with hyaluronic acid (HA) injection; 250 patients received MSC, 111 placebo injection, and 77 HA. Studies used either bone marrow (n=5), adipose tissue (n=6), or umbilical cord (n=2) as the source.MSC was not superior to either comparator with regards to patients exceeding the minimal clinically important difference (e.g. having a clinically meaningful benefit).

Hyaluronic acid injection has not been shown to be more effective than placebo in long-term studies. In one RCT of patients with symptomatic hip DJD, intra-articular injection of hyaluronic acid was no better than placebo.

A high quality systematic review found that in 18 large, adequately controlled trials with blinded outcome assessment (n = 5093 patients), there was no clinically significant benefit. The study also found evidence of more flare-ups and more serious adverse events.

For patients with OA of the trapeziometacarpal joint (base of thumb), there is no clear evidence favoring one surgical procedure over another, although the addition of ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition increases the likelihood of complications.

A systematic review of 6 trials (577 patients) concluded that Injection of platelet-rich plasma (PRP, compared to normal saline or hyaluronic acid) significantly improved knee function after 24 weeks, but not pain nor patient satisfaction among adults with knee osteoarthritis. The PRP groups had higher rates of non-severe and self-limited adverse events.

However in a 5 year follow-up of 192 patients initially randomized to PRP injection or hyaluronic acid injections, patients with unilateral mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis had comparable degrees of improvement. Given the limited benefit of viscosupplementation in adequately controlled randomized trials, this suggests a lack of benefit to PRP.

An RCT of 288 patients with symptomatic medial knee OA (Kellgren and Lawrence grade 2 or 3) randomized them to PRP injection or saline placebo injection. At 12 months, both groups had small and similar reductions in knee pain scores (-2.1 vs - 1.8 points, p = 0.17). There was also no change in medial tibial cartilage volume; 29 of 31 secondary outcomes showed no difference between groups.
A randomized trial comparing PRP injections with placebo injections in patients with ankle OA (n=100) found no difference in any outcomes.
A trial randomizing patients to leukocyte-rich plasma versus leukocyte poor plasma found no difference in outcomes. The trial did not have a control group.
A randomized trial found a greater likelihood of clinically significant improvement in moderately severe knee OA in those given autologous adipose derived platelet-rich plasma injections (NNT = 7).
A meta-analysis of 8 studies found some benefits for PRP injections in patients with hip OA, but studies were of poor quality and the differences were of borderline clinical signficance.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 18 randomized trials evaluated platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections for knee osteoarthritis. While the overall analysis suggested clinical improvements in pain and function, this was driven largely by lower-quality studies. When restricted to the 7 studies with a low risk of bias, PRP injections demonstrated no statistically significant reduction in pain at any follow-up interval (1, 3, 6, or 12 months). Functional improvement (WOMAC score) was seen only after 12 months.

In an RCT, dextrose prolotherapy (e.g. injecting dextrose as an irritant into the joint space to promote healing) was associated with better overall improvement in pain, stiffness and function compared to home exercise or intra-articular saline injection among patients with moderate to severe pain and radiographically confirmed knee OA. Between 82 and 91% of treated patients in all three groups would recommend their treatment to others.

In a study or 76 patients with knee OA and moderately severe pain, intra-articular injections with hypertonic dextrose (5 ml 25% dextrose) were slightly more effective than normal saline at improving the WOMAC score, but this difference of 10 points was of marginal clinical significance.

An industry sponsored trial found small improvements in pain at 12 weeks for joint injection with trans-capsaicin 1 mg compared with placebo. However, they had changed the outcome measure compared with their original protocol, and the differences are of questionable clinical significance. The injections were also quite painful and required repeated cooling and lidocaine injections (capsaicin is after all the active ingredient in pepper!).

A network meta-analysis of 21 studies with 1818 patients concluded that radiofrequency ablation was similarly effective to other therapies for knee OA including NSAIDs and other intra-articular injections. Cooled monopolar radiofrequency ablation was most effective in the SUCRA analysis.
The 2019 American College of Rheumatology made strong recommendations in favor of tai chi and conditional recommendations for yoga.
A 2025 randomized trial of 117 adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis found that a 24-week yoga program was noninferior to standard strengthening exercise therapy for reducing knee pain.

Controversy exists about the effectiveness of glucosamine. In some studies, glucosamine reduces the pain of moderate to severe OA of the knee, improves function, and can slow the progression of joint space narrowing. Onset of benefit is about 4 weeks. A Cochrane review found that glucosamine as a Rotta-brand pharmaceutical preparation was effective in the above parameters but non-Rotta preparations appear to be ineffective.

In a randomized controlled clinical trail with 164 patients, after 6 months of treatment, glucosamine plus chondroitin sulfate was no better than placebo in improving pain and function in patients with symptomatic knee degenerative joint disease (DJD).

A network meta-analysis of 47 randomized controlled trials (22,037 patients) on pharmacological treatments for long-term pain control (>12 months), physical function and joint structure in patients with knee OA demonstrated a decrease in pain with glucosamine sulfate (SMD - 0.29); improvements in joint space narrowing were found for glucosamine sulfate (SMD - 0.42), chondroitin sulfate (SMD - 0.20) and strontium ranelate (SMD - 0.20).
Studies of glucosamine concluded that is not effective for hip OA. or degenerative lumbar osteoarthritis.
S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe) reduces pain. However, it is expensive, and may cause several central nervous system side effects.
Acupuncture reduces pain and improves function. However, the placebo effect may play an important role as many trials are not well controlled with an effective sham therapy.

Magnet therapy may improve symptoms of OA, but the effect is lost after 6 weeks of therapy. In a systematic review, there was improvement in activities of daily living. A recent Cochrane review concluded that electromagnetic field therapy may provide moderate pain relief among patients with OA.
Ionized wrist bracelets called Q-Ray are no more effective than placebo in reducing musculoskeletal pain.
Ginger may provide a small benefit.
Avocado/soybean unsaponifiables have been shown to reduce pain and NSAID use in knee OA.
Low-level laser light therapy has been studied in five trials with about 400 patients; results are very mixed and trial quality was poor.
Topical therapies including arnica gel are probably as effective as topical gels with NSAIDs in symptom relief but with a potentially worse adverse event profile.
Supplementation with 2 grams of krill oil per day is no more effective than placebo for reducing pain in adults with knee OA.
Resveratrol (40 mg BID) showed no benefit over placebo for knee osteoarthritis pain (-15.7 vs. -15.2/100 at 3 months) or function.
Refer for assistive devices patients with restrictions of their activities of daily living.
Use occupational therapy for hand-related or specific work-related issues; use physical therapy for all other patients.

The 2019 American College of Rheumatology guidelines make strong recommendations for a comprehensive approach to hip or knee OA that includes exercise, self-efficacy programs, weight loss, tai chi, and assistive devices (eg, canes, tibiofemoral knee braces, and thumb splints). The panel made conditional recommendations in favor of education, cognitive behavioral therapy, and other forms of exercise.

A Cochrane review concluded that both high-intensity and low-intensity aerobic exercises are beneficial for the improvement of functional status, pain, gait, and aerobic capacity for patients with knee OA. Resistance training may also be of benefit.

However, among 377 participants randomized to high-intensity strength training addressing thigh muscle weakness (n = 127) no important differences were noted in knee OA outcomes compared to to low-intensity training or an attention control.
For patients with hip OA, there is limited evidence that supports a reduction in pain with exercise but no benefit on function.
Tai chi has been shown to improve symptoms in older women with OA.

An open label study randomized 156 adults with OA of the knee to up to 3 injections of 40 mg triamcinolone or up to 8 physical therapy sessions. Improvement in the WOMAC score was significantly greater in the PT group (56 vs 37 points).

In an unblinded study, about 50% of 189 patients with pain and function loss due to knee osteoarthritis who engaged in knee specific exercise therapy three times weekly for 12 weeks, experience clinically meaningful improvement in multiple outcome measurements. However 23% of the study participants dropped out after 3 months.

A 2025 network meta-analysis identifies aerobic exercise as the most effective modality for reducing pain and improving function in knee osteoarthritis, particularly in the short term. While neuromotor exercises (e.g., dancing) specifically improve gait and mind-body exercises offer acute pain relief, clinical benefits across all modalities tend to wane after six months, making patient enjoyment and adherence the most critical factors for long-term success.
Physical therapy is noninferior to arthroscopic partial menisectomy (APM) for improving patient-reported knee function in patients with non-obstructive (ie, no knee joint locking) meniscal tears.
Taping by physical therapists improves symptoms, and the benefits persist for up to 3 weeks after taping is stopped.

A Cochrane review of continuous passive motion following total knee arthroplasty in patients with arthritis found 24 RCTs with 1445 participants. Overall, the authors concluded that there was no good evidence that this interventions improved pain, function, range of motion, or quality of life.

Weekly sessions of total body Swedish massage, with significant attention to the lower extremities, were more effective than usual care or sham massages in reducing pain and improving function in patients with osteoarthritis of the knee. The benefit was sustained over 1 year, even when the massages were discontinued after 8 weeks.
A systematic review found no evidence that transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) is effective in pain control for knee OA. Studies were heterogeneous and of poor quality.
A systematic review of therapeutic ultrasound found mixed evidence to support its efficacy for patients with OA of the knee.
Small short-term benefits have been noted with aquatic therapy in patients with knee and hip osteoarthritis with regards to pain (SMD −0.31), disability(SMD −0.32) and quality of life (SMD −0.25).

In treating knee osteoarthritis aquatic exercise is comparable to light and-based exercise for pain relief, physical function and improvements in the quality of life, however adherence and satisfaction for aquatic-based exercises was higher than for land-based exercises.
There is some evidence to support the use of a knee braces to reduce pain and improve function in patients with knee OA.

Likewise there is limited evidence of reduced pain medication with use of pronation foot orthotics for medial knee OA. However, a recent systematic review concluded that there is minimal, if any, benefit to using a lateral wedge insoles (with at least 5 degrees to 15 degrees of angulation vs neutral or plat insoles) to reduce pain in adults with predominantly medial knee OA.
A randomized trial with 164 patients concluded that stable supportive shoes were slightly better at reducing knee pain (1.1 units on an 11 point scale) than flat, flexible shoes.

In a randomized trial of 220 adults with symptomatic knee OA, the use of biomechanical footwear (2 convex pods in the outsoles, calibrated to alter limb biomechanics and reduce stress on knees) statistically significantly reduced pain compared with control footwear. The overall mean pain reduction score was approximately 1 on a visual analog scale of 0–10 which is of borderline clinical significance.
Ice massage can improve range of motion and function in knee OA, but there is no evidence for a benefit on pain.
Balneotherapy, in particular mineral baths may reduce pain in patients with OA but evidence is limited.

In adults with moderate to severe knee pain due to DJD, a randomized trial with 64 patients concluded that ultrasound guided genicular nerve blocks provide 2 to 4 weeks of clinically meaningful pain relief compared with placebo.

Electrically heated mittens did not significantly improve hand function in osteoarthritis (AUSCAN function: +3.0 points, 95% CI -0.4 to 6.3, P = 0.09). A small reduction in hand pain was observed (+5.9 points, 95% CI 2.2 to 9.5), but no benefits were seen for overall osteoarthritis problems or grip strength.
Obese patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty can have similar long-term outcomes as non-obese patients.
Risk factors for revision include younger age and male sex for hip and knee arthroplasty. B
Symptoms wax and wane but typically progress over time. C
Symptoms of OA can wax and wane; degeneration of the joint progresses with aging.Obesity and weight gain can lead to further stress and destruction of the joint.

In one French general practice database, 52.3% of patients with knee OA had a flair-up. The authors created a flair-up score to define a flair-up using a rheumatology database as their gold standard (where 45.7% of patients were diagnosed by the rheumatologist with a flair-up).

Any structural lesion in the knee, as identified by MRI scanning, was present in up to 97% of symptomatic patients and 88% of asymptomatic patients (average age of 62.3 years), in a population-based observation study among 710 patients over the age of 50. Osteophytes were present in 74%, cartilage damage in 69%, and bone marrow lesions in 52%.
Obese patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty can have similar long-term outcomes as nonobese patients. However, a systematic review found function worse for obese patients after surgery.

A systematic review with meta-analysis that included 4811 procedures and 4263 patients concluded that high physical activity level is not associated with an increase in the need for total knee replacement revisions during the first 12 years after surgery and may be protective.

In a systematic review of 64 studies of hip and knee arthroplasty for OA, younger age and male sex increased the risk of revision 3-fold to 5-fold for hip and knee arthroplasty. Mortality was associated with older age and function was also worse for older patients after hip arthroplasty (particularly in women).

Following total knee arthroplasty, limited evidence from a meta-analysis of 6 observational studies found no evidence that higher levels of activity are associated with a greater likelihood of requiring reviion.

In a systematic review of hip OA, progression was most strongly associated with age, joint space width at entry into care, femoral head migration, femoral osteophytes, bony sclerosis, Kellgren/Lawrence hip grade 3, baseline hip pain, and Lequesne index score ≥10.

A 2025 randomized trial using hypothetical scenarios found that patients were more likely to believe they needed surgery if their diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis was supported by an x-ray (either described or shown) compared to receiving a clinical explanation alone. While x-ray use increased the perceived need for surgery, it did not alter patients' beliefs regarding the helpfulness of exercise or physical activity.
Wear cushioned shoes and replace them at regular intervals.
Exercise on softer surfaces.
Activities that promote joint motion with decreased weight bearing, such as cycling or swimming, reduce pain.
Weight loss decreases joint load and can decrease symptoms.
Avoid overusing/abusing joints.
Use heat or cold to reduce stiffness.

algorithm.title: Suggested treatment approach to the patient with osteoarthritis

cell.label: First-line treatments: full-dose acetaminophen, topical therapies, exercise, tai chi, knee taping, physical therapy.

Fourth-line treatments: carefully supervised opiates (50 mg of hydrocodone or 30 mg of oxycodone per day or less); joint replacement in patients with moderate to severe pain and moderate to severe radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis.
